curriculum.lesson_evidence: When you paint, how you hold and move the brush changes the marks you make. A flat stroke with the side of the brush covers a wide area, a tip stroke makes a fine line and dabbing with a nearly dry brush makes a rough texture. Mix colours on a palette, not on your picture, and rinse the brush between colours so they stay clean. Cover your table, wear a smock and wash up carefully. Light colours go on first and dark details are added last.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
You are painting a field of flowers under a blue sky. Plan which strokes and mixed colours you will use for the sky, the flowers and the stems, and in what order.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Sky first with wide flat strokes and a pale blue made with white, then green stems with a thin tip stroke, then dabs of pink and yellow for flowers.' Large light areas come first, then details, and each colour is mixed on the palette.

WATCH FOR
Thinking that painting means pressing the brush hard and adding thick paint everywhere. Too much paint hides the colours underneath and makes muddy mixes, so use light pressure and let layers dry when you want sharp edges.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.
